the presence of a solitary mass in the orbit should always be considered as a metastatic deposit from a primary lesion, and not as a primary lesion in itself, especially if the patient is in the age group of 50–65 years.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the diagnosis of lung cancer should be considered in patients presenting with an orbital lesion, even if there is no history of lung symptoms.
the presence of orbital metastasis from lung carcinoma should be considered as a possibility in patients with orbital symptoms and a lung mass.
metastasis from lung carcinoma should be considered as a differential for orbital swelling, especially in patients with a history of smoking, and should be investigated with a chest X-ray.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of an isolated metastasis in the orbit should raise suspicion for an occult primary cancer and should prompt a thorough investigation.
orbital metastasis from lung carcinoma may be the initial presenting feature of lung carcinoma and should be considered as a differential diagnosis in the appropriate clinical setting.
